frontmatter.title: Circuit Breaker
frontmatter.description: Protect your application from cascading failures with per-host circuit breaker. Stops requests when services are unhealthy, tests recovery with half-open probes.

core-api/circuit-breaker.html:
The Circuit Breaker protects downstream services from being overwhelmed by failing requests. When a host exceeds its failure threshold, the circuit opens and all subsequent requests fail immediately instead of retrying into a dead service.

Retry handles transient failures. Circuit breaker handles persistent failures.

Basic Usage

Configuration

Circuit States

                 ┌─────────────────┐
          ┌─────→│     CLOSED      │←────── Normal operation
          │      │ Requests flow   │       All requests succeed
          │      └────────┬────────┘
          │               │ Failures exceed threshold
          │               ↓
          │      ┌─────────────────┐
          │      │      OPEN       │←────── Emergency
          │      │ Requests fail   │       Requests rejected immediately
          │      │ Wait resetTimeout│
          │      └────────┬────────┘
          │               │ Timeout expires
          │               ↓
          │      ┌─────────────────┐
          │      │    HALF-OPEN    │←────── Probing
          │      │ Limited probes  │       Testing if service recovered
          │      └────────┬────────┘
          │               │
          ├─── Probes succeed ───→ CLOSED (recovered)
          └─── Probe fails ──────→ OPEN (still broken)

Per-Host Isolation

Circuit breakers are per-host. If api-primary.example.com fails, requests to api-backup.example.com continue unaffected:

Real-World Use Case: Microservice Dependencies

Circuit Breaker + Retry

Retries and circuit breaker work together:

  • Retries handle transient failures (single blips)
  • Circuit breaker handles sustained failures (service is down)

Error Handling

When the circuit is open, requests throw immediately:

Monitoring Circuit State

Use SolvixBus to react to circuit state changes:

Or use the onCircuitOpen hook:

Health Check Integration

Combine circuit breaker with health checks for proactive recovery detection:

When the health check succeeds, the circuit breaker can recover faster than waiting for resetTimeout.

Best Practices

  1. Set reasonable thresholds — 5–10 failures with 10–30s windows for most services
  2. Use retry alongside circuit breaker — retry for blips, circuit breaker for outages
  3. Per-host isolation — one bad service shouldn't affect others
  4. Half-open probes — always test before fully closing; services may need gradual warm-up
  5. Monitor circuit state — alerts on circuit open are a sign of production issues

frontmatter.title: ETag / Conditional Requests
frontmatter.description: Reduce bandwidth with conditional GET requests using ETag headers. Cache-aware, automatic.

core-api/etag-support.html:
Solvix supports ETag-based conditional requests. When enabled, Solvix stores the ETag response header and sends it as If-None-Match on subsequent requests. If the resource hasn't changed, the server returns 304 Not Modified and Solvix returns the cached response.

Don't re-download unchanged resources. ETags save bandwidth and improve latency.

Basic Usage

How It Works

First Request:
GET /large-data
← 200 OK, ETag: "abc123", { data: [...] }
→ Store: "/large-data" → ETag "abc123", response data

Second Request:
GET /large-data
If-None-Match: "abc123"
← 304 Not Modified (body empty)
→ Return stored response (same as first)

ETag + In-Memory Cache

Combine with cache for two-layer caching:

Best Practices

  1. Combine with cache — in-memory cache for rapid repeat access, ETag for cache revalidation
  2. Works best for large, infrequently-changing resources — API responses, config files, static data
  3. ETags are per-URL — different URLs have independent ETag stores
  4. No TTL configuration needed — ETags are always fresh until the server says otherwise

frontmatter.title: Middleware System
frontmatter.description: Extend Solvix with custom Koa-style middleware. Modify requests, responses, and context in the pipeline.

core-api/middleware-system.html:
Solvix supports Koa-style middleware — async functions that receive the request context and a next() callback. Middleware can modify the request before it's sent, the response after it's received, or wrap the entire pipeline.

Interceptors are a good idea, but middleware is better. Middleware composes — interceptors stack linearly.

Basic Middleware

How Middleware Works

Middleware follows the onion model — code before await next() runs on the way in (before the request), code after runs on the way out (after the response):

Request → [middleware 1] → [middleware 2] → [transport] → [middleware 2] → [middleware 1] → Response
               ↓                ↓                           ↑                  ↑
            pre-req          pre-req                     post-resp         post-resp

Real-World Use Cases

Auth Token Injection

Request Logging

Error Handling Wrapper

Response Transformation

Request Retry with Delay

Middleware + Solvix Features

Middleware runs inside the retry loop, before the transport. This means:

  • Middleware runs on every retry attempt
  • Middleware can modify ctx.url and ctx.options — changes persist across retries
  • Middleware cannot bypass the circuit breaker or rate limiter (they run before the retry loop)
Retry Loop:
  → Rate Limit Check
  → Circuit Breaker Check
  → Middleware Stack (user-defined)
  → Transport (fetch/custom)
  → Response/Error → Retry? → back to top

Middleware Order

Middleware is executed in the order it was registered:

Error Handling in Middleware

If a middleware throws, subsequent middleware and the transport are skipped:

Middleware vs Hooks

Feature Middleware Hooks
Can modify request ✅ Yes ⚠️ Limited
Can modify response ✅ Yes ❌ No
Can block/abort ✅ Yes ❌ No
Runs on retries ✅ Yes ✅ Yes
Use case Transformations, auth, validation Logging, monitoring, metrics

Best Practices

  1. Always call await next() — otherwise the request stops at your middleware
  2. Keep middleware focused — one concern per middleware
  3. Handle errors — wrap await next() in try/catch for error tracking
  4. Don't mutate ctx.options.group — it's used by the request group system
  5. Test middleware independently — create a mock context and call your middleware with it

frontmatter.title: Offline Queue
frontmatter.description: Queue requests when offline and replay them when connectivity returns. Browser-focused with optional persistence.

core-api/offline-queue.html:
The Offline Queue saves outgoing requests when the browser is offline and automatically replays them when connectivity is restored.

Your app shouldn't crash when the network drops. Queue it, replay it, move on.

Basic Usage

When the browser goes offline, requests are queued instead of failing:

Configuration

Persistence

With persist: true, the queue survives page reloads:

This means queued requests that weren't sent before the user closed the tab will be replayed when they return.

How It Works

  1. Browser detects connectivity change (navigator.onLine)
  2. When offline: fetch fails → request is serialized and queued
  3. When online: queue is flushed — requests are replayed in FIFO order
  4. Failed replays are retried (if retry is configured) or dropped

Real-World Use Case: Analytics Tracking

Offline Queue + Retry

When replayed, queued requests use the client's retry configuration:

Browser Support

Feature Chrome Firefox Safari Edge
Offline detection ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅
Request queueing ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅
Persistence (localStorage) ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅

Best Practices

  1. Enable persist for analytics — don't lose user activity data
  2. Set maxQueueSize — prevents unbounded memory growth during extended offline periods
  3. Combine with retry — replays may fail if the server was also temporarily down
  4. Use for non-critical requests — mutations queued offline may be stale by the time they're replayed
  5. Test offline behavior — use DevTools > Network > Offline to simulate

Rate limiting at the client prevents 429s before they happen.

Request 1:   consume 1 → 9 tokens remaining
Request 2:   consume 1 → 8 tokens remaining
...
Request 10:  consume 1 → 0 tokens remaining
Request 11:  WAIT for refill → 1 token available → consume → 0 remaining

X-RateLimit-Limit: 60
X-RateLimit-Remaining: 42

frontmatter.title: Request Deduplication
frontmatter.description: Automatically deduplicate identical in-flight requests. 1000 concurrent calls → 1 network request.

core-api/request-deduplication.html:
When dedupe is enabled, Solvix prevents redundant network calls. If a request with the same method, URL, body, and headers is already in-flight, subsequent calls share the same Promise — the result is broadcast to all callers.

The classic "1000 concurrent identical requests → 1 actual network call" feature.

Basic Usage

Now 100 concurrent calls to the same endpoint:

How It Works

Solvix generates a SHA-256 fingerprint of the request (method, URL, body, headers). In-flight requests are stored in a map keyed by this fingerprint:

Request A: GET /users → fingerprint("GET|/users||") → store Promise
Request B: GET /users → fingerprint("GET|/users||") → return same Promise
Request C: GET /users → fingerprint("GET|/users||") → return same Promise

Response received → resolve all 3 promises → 1 network call total

SHA-256 is only computed when dedupe or cache is enabled — no performance impact when disabled.

Cache Integration

Dedup works before the cache check:

Dedup Check ──→ Hit? → return in-flight Promise
   ↓ Miss
Cache Check ──→ Hit? → return cached response
   ↓ Miss
Network Request → store in cache → return response

This means a request that was just completed (cached) won't trigger a new network call even if another request comes in before the cache TTL expires.

Dedup + Retry

Deduplicated requests share the same retry lifecycle:

Dedup + Token Refresh

When token refresh is configured, dedup also applies to the refresh operation itself — the classic "100 concurrent 401s → 1 token refresh" pattern:

Per-Request Exclusion

To skip dedup for a specific request:

Fingerprint Customization

Use fingerprint to customize the dedup key:

Memory Safety

The in-flight registry evicts entries FIFO at 10,000 to prevent memory leaks in long-running processes.

Performance Impact

Scenario Requests Network Calls Saved
1000 users load dashboard 1000 1 99.9%
Retry storm 500 ~3 (1 per retry) 99.4%
No dedup 100 100 0%

Best Practices

  1. Enable globally for GET requests — idempotent reads benefit most
  2. Disable for POST/PUT/PATCH — mutations shouldn't be deduped (unless idempotent)
  3. Combine with retry — dedup + retry = efficient failure recovery
  4. Monitor dedup hit rate — a high hit rate means your UI is making too many duplicate calls

core-api/retry-engine.html:
The Retry Engine automatically retries failed requests using configurable strategies. It integrates with the circuit breaker, rate limiter, and deduplication system — retries never overwhelm failing services.

Don't build retry wrappers. Solvix retries are built-in, composable, and production-tested under 50 concurrent failures.

Configuration

Complete Example

How it Works

Request fails ──→ shouldRetry? ──→ No ──→ Throw error
                       │
                      Yes
                       ↓
         Wait: delay = min(baseDelay * factor^attempt, maxTimeout)
         Apply jitter: delay ± 25%
                       ↓
         Adapt: maxTimeout = max(maxTimeout, actualNetworkTime * 2)
                       ↓
         Retry request (circuit breaker check → queue → transport)
                       ↓
         Success? ──→ Return response
         Fail? ──→ Loop back

frontmatter.title: Architecture Overview
frontmatter.description: How Solvix's request pipeline works — every stage a request passes through from creation to completion.

getting-started/architecture-overview.html:
Solvix processes every request through a structured pipeline — a sequence of stages that handle security, queuing, resilience, transport, and observability. Each stage is optional and only runs when its feature is configured.

Pipeline Diagram

Request Created
      ↓
Security Checks ─── HTTPS enforcement, domain/method allowlisting,
                      header sanitization, CRLF protection, size guards
      ↓
Query Parameter Processing ─── params merge, custom paramsSerializer
      ↓
Fingerprinting ─── SHA-256 key for dedup/cache (skipped when unused)
      ↓
Deduplication Check ─── If dedupe enabled: return in-flight promise
      ↓
Cache Check ─── If cache enabled: return cached response
      ↓
Dependency Wait ─── If dependsOn set: wait for dependencies
      ↓
Priority Queue ─── If maxConcurrency set: queue + schedule
      ↓
Rate Limiter ─── If rate limit enabled: acquire token
      ↓
Circuit Breaker ─── If circuit breaker enabled: check health
      ↓
Retry Loop ═══════════════════════════════════════════════╗
   ↓                                                        ║
   ├─ Header Sanitization (always on)                      ║
   ├─ Request Body Construction                             ║
   ├─ Middleware Stack (user-defined)                       ║
   ├─ Transport Execution (fetch / custom transport)        ║
   ├─ Response Parsing (JSON, text, stream, etc.)          ║
   ├─ Response Validation (if validateResponse set)        ║
   ├─ Cache Storage (if cache enabled, GET only)           ║
   └─ Error → Retry? → Yes → back to ═════════════════════╝
                         No  ↓
Response Returned
      ↓
Events Emitted ─── SolvixBus: request:complete / request:error
      ↓
Logging ─── Structured log via configured logger
      ↓
Metrics Update ─── Counters + histograms updated
      ↓
Health Check Tick ─── If health check enabled: update stats

Key Design Principles

1. Opt-In Architecture

No feature adds overhead unless configured. A bare client with no options is equivalent to native fetch in performance — just with security guards always active.

2. Composition Over Configuration

Complex behaviors are built by composing small, focused stages. Retry logic composes with circuit breaker. Rate limiting respects queue priority. Dedup is cache-aware.

3. Observer Pattern

Every stage emits events through SolvixBus. You can observe, log, and monitor every request without modifying the pipeline.

4. Transport Agnostic

The transport layer is swappable. The default is fetch, but you can provide a custom SolvixTransport for HTTP/2, gRPC, WebSocket, or mock transports.

Middleware Architecture

Middleware runs inside the retry loop, before the transport. This means middleware changes are preserved across retries, and middleware can implement its own retry logic.

Middleware uses a Koa-style onion model — code before await next() runs on the way in, code after runs on the way out.

Event-Driven Extensibility

SolvixBus emits typed events at key lifecycle points:

  • request:start — request entered the pipeline
  • request:retry — about to retry
  • request:complete — successful response
  • request:error — permanent failure
  • health:change — health checker detected state change
  • request:shadow* — shadow request lifecycle

frontmatter.title: Design Goals
frontmatter.description: The principles and design philosophy behind Solvix.

getting-started/design-goal.html:
Solvix was designed from the ground up with specific goals that shaped its architecture.

1. Zero-Cost Abstraction

Features you don't use should cost nothing. A bare createClient() with no options should perform identically to native fetch — and it does.

How: Every feature wraps a no-op when disabled. SHA-256 hashing for dedup keys is skipped entirely when dedupe and cache are both off. The priority queue defaults to Infinity concurrency, acting as a direct pass-through.

2. TypeScript First, Not TypeScript Only

The entire library is written in TypeScript with strict: true. But the public API is fully typed for consumers in both JS and TS — you get autocomplete either way.

How: All option interfaces use generics. client.get<T>() infers response types. validateResponse integrates with Zod/Valibot schemas without requiring them.

3. Resilience by Composition

Individual resilience patterns (retry, circuit breaker, rate limiting) are well-understood. Solvix's innovation is making them compose correctly — retries respect rate limits, circuit breakers track retry failures, dedup is cache-aware.

How: The pipeline architecture ensures stages execute in order. Downstream stages (like the circuit breaker) see the aggregated state from upstream stages (like retry attempts).

4. Transparent Observability

You should never wonder "what happened" to a request. Timeline, profiling, correlation IDs, and structured logging are built into the core — not added as afterthoughts.

How: The SolvixContext object that flows through every stage accumulates metadata. The final response always carries meta.timeline, meta.profile, and meta.correlationId if enabled.

5. Enterprise Security by Default

The most common security issues in HTTP clients (CRLF injection, header smuggling, sensitive data in snapshots) are handled automatically. Additional layers are opt-in.

How: Header sanitization runs on every request (strips Host, Connection, Transfer-Encoding). Snapshot mode automatically redacts sensitive headers.

6. Transport Agnosticism

The HTTP transport should be swappable without changing application code. Whether you're using fetch, undici, http2, or a mock transport for testing, the API stays the same.

How: The SolvixTransport type is a simple (url, init) => Promise<Response> signature. Proxy and TLS features use undici under the hood but expose the same API.

7. Minimum Dependencies

Zero runtime dependencies (except optional undici for proxy/TLS). The entire library is self-contained, auditable, and easy to bundle.

How: SHA-256 uses the Web Crypto API (built into all runtimes). Priority queue is hand-rolled (binary heap, not a library). No lodash, no tslib, no polyfills.

8. Universal Runtime Support

The same API works in Node.js, browsers, Deno, Bun, and edge runtimes. No platform-specific code paths in the public API.

How: Uses fetch which is available in all modern runtimes. Proxy/TLS features are isolated to a node/ module and only imported when configured.

Non-Goals

  • Not a replacement for WebSocket/SSE clients — Solvix handles HTTP requests. For persistent connections, use the appropriate client.
  • Not a full OpenAPI client — Solvix doesn't generate code from OpenAPI specs. It's a runtime HTTP client.
  • Not a GraphQL client — Solvix can send GraphQL requests but doesn't parse GraphQL schemas.

Solvix is a TypeScript-first HTTP orchestration engine — not just an HTTP client. It transforms simple API requests into secure, observable, resilient, and fully controlled execution pipelines.

Unlike traditional HTTP clients (Axios, Got, Ky) that leave resilience, security, and observability to the developer, Solvix bakes ~50 features into a single 33 KB package.

There are many HTTP clients in the JavaScript ecosystem. Here's why Solvix exists and what makes it different.

The Problem with Traditional HTTP Clients

Most HTTP clients focus on one thing: sending requests and receiving responses. Everything else — retries, security, observability, queue management — is left to the developer.

Result: Production codebases end up with ad-hoc retry wrappers, manual token refresh logic, scattered logging, and inconsistent error handling.

HTTP proxy + custom TLS ✅ (via undici) ✅ ✅ ❌ ❌

Where Solvix Excels

1. Fully Integrated Pipeline

In Solvix, every feature plugs into a single request pipeline. Retries interact with the circuit breaker. Rate limiting respects queue priority. Deduplication is aware of caching. Features don't fight each other — they compose.

2. True Observability

Solvix doesn't just send requests — it traces them. Every request gets a correlation ID, a W3C traceparent header, a 15-stage timeline, and performance metrics. You can subscribe to lifecycle events globally via SolvixBus.

3. Enterprise Security by Default

CRLF injection protection, forbidden header stripping, and snapshot redaction are always on. Additional layers (HTTPS enforcement, domain allowlisting, CSRF protection, size guards) are one config field away.

4. No External Dependencies

Solvix has zero runtime dependencies (except undici for proxy/TLS features, which is optional). The entire library is a single, self-contained build.

Where Solvix Differs in Philosophy

  • Opt-in, not opt-out — features are disabled by default. You enable what you need.
  • Observability-first — every feature emits events, logs, and metrics automatically.
  • Middleware over configuration — complex logic goes into custom middleware, not config bloat.
  • Transport-agnostic — swap out the underlying HTTP transport without changing your code.

When to Use Solvix

Solvix is ideal for:

  • Large-scale frontend applications with complex API needs
  • Backend services requiring resilience patterns
  • Multi-runtime projects (Node.js + browser + edge)
  • Enterprise systems with strict security requirements
  • Microservices architectures with observability needs

When Not to Use Solvix

For extremely simple use cases (a single GET request to a public API), native fetch is perfectly fine. Solvix adds value when you need resilience, security, and observability at scale.
